title: The proud fall
hook: the one who is proud of power will fall (Sukhmani 12)

segments.voice: Yesterday, nimrataa, humility: set the self down, and the humble rest easy. Today the twelfth ashtpadi shows the other side of the coin.

Guru Arjan makes a list in the first stanza of the twelfth ashtpadi, and it reads like a lineup of the people the world envies. The one with power. The one who is young and good-looking. The one with money and land. You'd expect a hymn about pride to stop there. It doesn't. Slipped into the same list, right beside the rich and the beautiful, is someone who seems to belong on the other team entirely: the person who is proud of being good.
screen: `POWER. YOUTH. MONEY AND LAND.` → `AND ONE MORE NAME ON THE LIST.` → `THE ONE PROUD OF BEING GOOD.`

segments.voice: Yesterday's salok said the proud are worn away by their own pride. Now the stanza shows what that pride looks like, one kind per line, each with a blunt picture of where it ends. Whoever carries the pride of ruling, the text says, sinks as low as a dog. Whoever thinks, I am young and beautiful, ends up a worm in filth. The images are harsh on purpose; Guru Arjan isn't polite about something he thinks is dangerous. Then the turn, before the stanza even reaches wealth: whoever calls himself a doer of good deeds wanders through birth after birth. Only then comes wealth: whoever is proud of money and land, he calls a blind, ignorant fool. The good-deeds line is the one that stops a reader. The Guru Granth Sahib praises good deeds, and Sikh life is full of them: serving in the langar, giving to people in need, standing up for the weak. So what's wrong with doing good? Nothing. The warning is about the calling yourself. Good done and then worn like a medal becomes the same as the crown and the bank account: something to stand on, something to be seen with. The salok's word for the proud was ahankaaree, from ahankaar, ego, the voice that says: I did this. The pride is the same in all four, and so is the fall. Pride needs height, and height means a drop. The bigger the pedestal, the farther down the floor.
screen: `POWER AND YOUTH: EACH FALLS.` · `BLUNT PICTURES, ON PURPOSE.` · `EVEN PRIDE IN GOOD DEEDS.` · `AHANKAAR: THE VOICE THAT SAYS I.` · then, large: `PRIDE FALLS.`

segments.voice: Sit quietly and let the mind run until it brings up something like, I handled that well, or I'm not like those people, or at least I'm the one who helps. When it does, don't scold it; notice it the way you'd notice a car going by, name it softly, pride, and let it pass. Even catching one is the practice.
Ahankaar, pride, ego. Pride of power, of youth, of wealth, and even of good deeds: the voice that says I did this, and every pedestal has a drop.
Your line: pride falls. Good done quietly needs no pedestal. Day four hundred eighty-three counts.

howItsDone: Sikhs reciting Sukhmani Sahib move through the stanzas of the twelfth ashtpadi, which name pride of power, beauty, wealth and good deeds, and Sikh teaching on seva prizes service done without show.

fork.setup: you've volunteered every weekend for a year. someone asks how you spend your Saturdays. by the twelfth ashtpadi, where's the danger?
options: in wearing the good deed like a medal.
there's no danger in good deeds at all.
fork.reveal: the stanza names whoever calls himself a doer of good deeds. the good is fine; the calling yourself is the pedestal.

original.note: Gurmukhi: ahankaar, pride, ego; the sense of making a me.

trapdoor: what you thought: pride is a rich person's problem.
what it means: pride is anything you stand on to be higher, even your own goodness.
what a scholar hears: ahankaar comes from Sanskrit ahamkara, aham, I, plus kara, making; Sikh teaching counts it among the five thieves.
guess: ego, the inner voice that says I did this
healthy confidence in your own abilities
anger at someone who has wronged you

chat.says: I volunteer every weekend. How could being proud of that be a problem?
options: Doing good is wonderful; Sukhmani warns about wearing it like a medal, the ego saying I did this.
Sukhmani says good deeds themselves are the problem, so it's better not to volunteer at all.
Pride is only a problem for the rich and powerful; good deeds can never feed the ego.
chat.meaning: The stanza says whoever calls himself a doer of good deeds wanders birth after birth; the deeds are praised, the self-praise is the trap.

ahankaar.meaning: ego, pride, the voice that says I did this

ahankaaree.meaning: a proud one, full of ego

Guru Arjan.meaning: the fifth Sikh Guru, who wrote Sukhmani

langar.meaning: the free community kitchen, served by volunteers

sources.ref: Sukhmani Sahib, ashtpadi 12, stanza 1 (Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 278)

notes: Ashtpadi 12 stanza 1 paraphrased: jis kai antar raaj abhimaan (dog), jo jaanai mai jobanvant (worm in filth), jo aapas kau karmavant kahaavai (wanders through births), dhan bhoom kaa jo karai gumaan (blind fool). Confirm the order and that all four lines sit in stanza 1.
Ahankaar from Sanskrit aham + kara and its place among the five thieves (kaam, krodh, lobh, moh, ahankaar): confirm.
Dasvandh (giving a tenth) mentioned in passing.
